name: Rapport
tagline: Success is needing the app less over time.
summary: A training system for practical communication skills: assess, learn, rehearse, practise for real, reflect, adapt. Deterministic systems own every number; the model only ever writes sentences.

authorship.role: Sole author — domain model, adaptive engine, simulator and evaluation.
built: The skill graph and its acyclicity/behavioural-definition constraints
The Kalman-style mastery model that tracks mastery and confidence separately, each with its own uncertainty
The ten-factor recommender, the conversation simulator and the transcript-feature evaluator
The event-log projection with scoring-model version stamps and history recomputation
notBuilt: The language models used for character dialogue and feedback wording
Supabase, used only as an opaque store for the optional end-to-end encrypted sync blob

caseStudy.problem: Social-skills apps tend to become either a chatbot you talk to forever or a personality test that hands you a label. Both fail the same way: they make the product the destination. If the tool is working, the user should need it less each month, which means it has to measure real-world behaviour rather than in-app engagement.
caseStudy.approach: Model skills as observable behaviours rather than traits, and track belief about each one as a distribution rather than a score — mastery and confidence separately, each with uncertainty that shrinks with evidence and widens with time. Keep every number deterministic and local; let the model play characters and rephrase feedback, but never let it produce a score. Scores computed from too little material are marked unreliable and never move mastery at all.

architecture.summary: A pure-TypeScript domain core with no I/O, wrapped by a thin AI boundary and a UI that renders what the core computed.
architecture.invariant: Deterministic systems own every number and every decision; the model only ever writes sentences. Skill states are a projection of an append-only event log, stamped with the scoring-model version that produced them.

layers.name: domain/
layers.role: Mastery model, recommender, evaluator, scheduler, safety gates, analytics and content. No I/O, no React, no model calls.

layers.name: ai/
layers.role: Provider abstraction, versioned prompts, schema-validated responses, cache, rate limiter, benchmark set.

layers.name: data/
layers.role: IndexedDB repository, append-only event log, export/wipe, end-to-end encrypted sync.

layers.name: state/
layers.role: One store. Every derived value recomputed from the event log rather than stored.

visuals.caption: Illustration of the skill-graph model. Not a screenshot — no capture of the running app has been published yet.

metrics.label: Skill graph
metrics.method: Content counted from the shipped skill graph. Graph integrity, acyclicity and behavioural definitions are asserted by the tests/skill-graph suite.

metrics.label: Test suites
metrics.method: Counted from the suite table in the README: skill-graph, mastery, evaluation, recommender, training-loop, analytics, safety, content, persistence, ai-eval, a11y, and an E2E suite. `npm run verify` runs lint, types, content validation, all unit suites and the production build.

outcomes.statement: The product works fully with no AI provider configured — scoring, recommendations, scheduling, insights and reviews are computed on device, and practice conversations fall back to a built-in character engine.

evidence.label: rapport.yml runs the whole verify suite and E2E with AI_PROVIDER=none

outcomes.statement: When the scoring model changes, the version stamp on a skill state mismatches and history is recomputed rather than left stale.
Insights are suppressed below a minimum sample size, and behaviour scores computed from too little material are marked unreliable and never move mastery.

tradeoffs.choice: Deterministic core owns every number; the model is confined to prose
tradeoffs.gained: Scores are reproducible and testable, the app degrades to full functionality with no provider, and a model outage cannot change anyone's mastery.
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Evaluation is limited to features that can be counted from a transcript, so it cannot judge the things a human coach would notice but cannot count.

tradeoffs.choice: Onboarding produces priors with wide uncertainty instead of a score
tradeoffs.gained: The app never hands someone a label off seven questions, and confidence genuinely grows with evidence.
tradeoffs.gaveUp: A less satisfying first run. There is no number to show off on day one, which is exactly what most competing products lead with.

tradeoffs.choice: Local-first with every permission off by default
tradeoffs.gained: Sensitive practice material stays on device; sync, when enabled, stores only an opaque encrypted blob.
tradeoffs.gaveUp: No cross-device continuity without deliberate setup, and no aggregate data to improve the model with.

lessons: Tracking mastery and confidence as one number collapses two different things — knowing how to do something and believing you can — and the product's whole reason to exist lives in the gap between them.
limitations: No longitudinal field study — transfer from simulator practice to real conversations is asserted by the design, never measured.
The human-rated evaluation pipeline holds zero external ratings so far.
The safety gate is deterministic pattern matching; no third-party adversarial red-team has audited it.
